$comment: EXAMPLE ONLY. Every key_sha256 below is a placeholder, not a real hash.
A key's secret is never written to this file -- only sha256(secret) is. Mint a
real key yourself (rh_turn_<43 base62 chars> or rh_admin_<43 base62 chars>,
32 CSPRNG bytes each), hash it, and replace the placeholder hex below with
that hash. The hashes here are sha256 of the literal placeholder strings
'REPLACE-with-a-real-turn-key-then-hash-it' and its admin counterpart, so
they parse and validate as an example but authenticate nothing: if you point
ROUNDHOUSE_CONTROL_PLANE at this file unmodified, every request resolves
unknown_key.
A project's "policy" sets what its turns may do: min_quality (0.0 = no
floor), allow (glob patterns over a target's identity -- "provider/model"
for a hosted model, "local/model" for one of the fleet's own; absent or
"*" admits everything), and frontier_cadence (at most max_frontier hosted
dispatches in a trailing window of per_turns turns; when the window is
spent, hosted targets go inadmissible and the turn serves locally instead
of failing). Absent "policy" means unrestricted -- the same routing this
deployment would do with no control plane at all.
Two things a cadence is not. It is not an allow-list: max_frontier of 0
forbids every hosted target on every turn and is rejected at load, naming
the entry and pointing at "allow": ["local/*"], which is how that is
written. And it is not a promise this file can keep by itself -- "serves
locally" needs a local fleet, so a deployment with none refuses to start
rather than failing every rationed session from its second turn onwards.
A key's "overrides" narrow its project's policy for that key alone, via
the same three axes. Narrowing only: an override that would raise the
admissible set on any axis -- a lower min_quality, a looser cadence -- is
rejected at load, naming both the key and the project it belongs to, rather
than silently clamped. Ada's key below tightens the floor from 0.5 to 0.8
and the cadence from 2-per-10 to 1-per-10; it could not loosen either.
A project's "budget" sets its spending ceiling: limit_usd, a window
("total" for the life of the project, "monthly" resetting each UTC
calendar month), on_exhaustion ("degrade_to_local" keeps serving from
the local fleet once the limit is spent, "refuse" stops the turn with a
retryable error), and warn_at (default 0.8 -- the fraction of the limit
past which a grant comes back marked Warned, before anything actually
degrades). "overflow_when_local_saturated" lives beside on_exhaustion
and only means something under degrade_to_local: when true (the default)
a turn that finds the local pool itself full is re-admitted to frontier
rather than failing, and the overspend is booked rather than hidden.
Setting it under "refuse" is rejected at load, naming the project --
overflow is a degrade-mode valve, and a project that refuses on
exhaustion never promised local service in the first place. Acme's
budget below spells the flag out explicitly, but true is also what an
absent flag would mean.
A key's "allocation" gives that membership its own ceiling on top of
its project's -- both bind, and the tighter one wins. Absent means
"pooled": no second ceiling, the key may spend up to the whole project
budget. "capped" is an absolute dollar figure; "share" is a fraction of
the project limit, so it tracks a later increase instead of freezing a
dollar amount. Shares are ceilings, not a partition: several keys' shares
may sum past 1.0, and the project limit is what stops all of them
together -- validation does not refuse an over-subscribed set of shares.
Bob's key below is capped at a flat $100; Cara's is a 25% share of
whatever acme's limit currently is.
A project's or a key's "fair_use" caps token and/or dollar draws over a
rolling window -- "5h", "24h" or "7d" -- shaped like a frontier lab's own
session limits, not a calendar reset like "budget" above. Each window needs
at least one of max_tokens or max_usd; an entry naming neither reads like a
limit and enforces nothing, and is rejected at load rather than silently
kept. It is a second axis from "budget", never a variant of it: a budget is
a ledger with a hold and a settlement, fair use is a rolling counter with
neither, and the two compose -- a project may carry both, either, or
neither. A key's own fair_use is a second ceiling on top of its project's,
never an overlay on it: both bind independently, and whichever is tighter
refuses first, naming its own scope ("project" or "member") and window in
the 429 rather than leaving a client to guess which one to raise. Acme's
project-level window below caps the whole project at 2,000,000 tokens per
rolling 5 hours; Bob's own window on top of it caps him individually at
400,000 tokens per rolling 24 hours, so his personal ceiling can refuse him
on a busy day even while Acme as a whole still has room. This milestone's
enforcement is single-node only -- see roundhouse_core::control::fair_use for
the unlock condition -- so a deployment running more than one process behind
ROUNDHOUSE_REDIS_URL gets two independent ceilings out of this, not one
shared one, until that lands; the process warns at boot when both apply.
Point ROUNDHOUSE_CONTROL_PLANE at your copy.
